    "https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto"
  ],
  "combined_key_facts": [
    "Cointelegraph says the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass, and that it risks not advancing at all if lawmakers miss the window before the midterms.",
    "NYDIG’s Greg Cipolaro says the realistic window is June through early August, after which the highest-probability path becomes a post-election lame-duck session if Republicans keep the Senate.",
    "The article says Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority and would need at least seven Democrats to reach the 60 votes needed to avoid prolonged debate and pass the bill.",
    "CoinDesk’s RSS item frames the same event as the Clarity Act taking a step forward after a contentious markup hearing, showing the bill is advancing but still faces major political friction.",
    "Cipolaro says a signed bill would give markets a boost and bring regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission."
  ],
  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. If the bill misses that window, he said the most likely remaining path is a post-election lame-duck session, and even that depends on Republicans retaining the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune prioritizing the measure over government funding deadlines. He also said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed version is unlikely to advance in the next Congress beginning in January. The article adds that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would likely benefit because major institutions would gain enough confidence to invest in the sector thanks to clearer rules. Cipolaro said the bill would also provide regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing what he called the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class. But he also warned the bill could still fail because negotiations could stall over ethics or decentralized finance enforcement language, or because scheduling delays could prevent action. CoinDesk’s RSS item for the same news cycle, titled “The Clarity Act took a step forward: State of Crypto,” described the issue as unpacking Thursday’s at-times contentious markup hearing. That framing matches Cointelegraph’s account of the Senate Banking Committee advancing the bill, but it emphasizes that the legislative move was only a step forward rather than final passage. Taken together, the two sources show a single dominant story: Congress advanced the crypto market-structure bill, but the path to law remains narrow, politically fragile, and highly sensitive to the Senate calendar. The shared theme is not just that the bill moved forward, but that the next several weeks may determine whether crypto regulation gets a breakthrough in 2026 or slips into a later political window. The market implication is important because the bill could give Bitcoin clearer treatment under federal law, while also opening the door to broader institutional participation if lawmakers can resolve the remaining disputes. The tone across both sources is cautious: progress is real, but the deadline pressure is increasing. Cointelegraph also noted that the industry is still operating under permanent jurisdictional ambiguity if the legislation stalls, which helps explain why the story matters beyond Washington. The bill is being watched as a signal for whether lawmakers can create a workable framework for the digital asset market, especially at a moment when both policy and market structure debates are moving quickly. The recurring facts across the feeds are the markup passage, the need for 60 votes, the seven-Democrat hurdle, the June-to-early-August window, the midterm risk, and the potential Bitcoin commodity classification. Those are the core details that define the event.",
  "CHART_COIN": "bitcoin"
}

# Senate crypto bill faces 60-vote August deadline

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the market structure measure may not clear Congress until August, and it still needs 60 votes to move cleanly through the chamber. That puts a hard number on the story, because the realistic window now runs from June through early August before recess and campaign politics squeeze floor time.

For traders, the read is less about an immediate price spike and more about probability. Republicans control 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed, and that makes every delay matter. If the bill slips past the summer window, the next likely shot is a lame-duck session rather than a normal fall push.

data.systemPrompt:
You are a personal assistant running inside OpenClaw.
## Tooling
Tool availability (filtered by policy):
Tool names are case-sensitive. Call tools exactly as listed.
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise edits to files
- exec: Run shell commands (pty available for TTY-required CLIs)
- process: Manage background exec sessions
- web_search: Search the web (Brave API)
- web_fetch: Fetch and extract readable content from a URL
- browser: Control web browser
- canvas: Present/eval/snapshot the Canvas
- message: Send messages and channel actions
- agents_list: List OpenClaw agent ids allowed for sessions_spawn when runtime="subagent" (not ACP harness ids)
- sessions_list: List other sessions (incl. sub-agents) with filters/last
- sessions_history: Fetch history for another session/sub-agent
- sessions_send: Send a message to another session/sub-agent
- subagents: List, steer, or kill sub-agent runs for this requester session
- session_status: Show a /status-equivalent status card (usage + time + Reasoning/Verbose/Elevated); use for model-use questions (📊 session_status); optional per-session model override
- image_generate: Generate images with the configured image-generation model
- memory_get
- memory_search
- sessions_spawn: Spawn a sub-agent or ACP coding session; defaults to isolated, native subagents may use context="fork" when current transcript context is required (runtime="acp" requires `agentId` unless `acp.defaultAgent` is configured; ACP harness ids follow acp.allowedAgents, not agents_list)
- sessions_yield
- tts
TOOLS.md does not control tool availability; it is user guidance for how to use external tools.
For long waits, avoid rapid poll loops: use exec with enough yieldMs or process(action=poll, timeout=<ms>).

### Heartbeats

The purpose of heartbeats is to make you feel magical and proactive. Come to life and start proactively doing things that are important.
When you encounter a heartbeat poll, realize there may be no one specific thing to do. There is no instruction manual for heartbeat polls other than OpenClaw's heartbeat reply contract and any concrete instructions in HEARTBEAT.md.

Have some variety in what you do when that creates more value. Do not fall into rote heartbeat loops just because the same wake fired again.

If HEARTBEAT.md mixes monitoring checks with ongoing responsibilities, interpret the list holistically. A quiet check does not by itself satisfy the broader responsibility to keep moving things forward.

If HEARTBEAT.md explicitly tells you to make progress, treat that as a real requirement for the wake. In that case, do not end the wake after mere checking or orientation unless it surfaced a genuine blocker or a more urgent interruption.
Use your judgment and be creative and tasteful with this process. Prefer meaningful action over commentary.
A heartbeat is not a status report. Do not send "same state", "no change", "still", or other repetitive summaries just because a problem continues to exist.

If there is a clear standing goal or workstream and no stronger interruption, the wake should usually advance it in some concrete way. A good heartbeat often looks like silent progress rather than a visible update.

  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. tools.name: agents_list
tools.description: List OpenClaw agent ids you can target with `sessions_spawn` when `runtime="subagent"` (based on subagent allowlists).

tools.name: browser
tools.description: Control the browser via OpenClaw's browser control server (status/start/stop/profiles/tabs/open/snapshot/screenshot/actions). Browser choice: omit profile by default for the isolated OpenClaw-managed browser (`openclaw`). For the logged-in user browser, use profile="user". A supported Chromium-based browser (v144+) must be running on the selected host or browser node. Use only when existing logins/cookies matter and the user is present. When a node-hosted browser proxy is available, the tool may auto-route to it. Pin a node with node=<id|name> or target="node". When using refs from snapshot (e.g. e12), keep the same tab: prefer passing targetId from the snapshot response into subsequent actions (act/click/type/etc). For stable, self-resolving refs across calls, use snapshot with refs="aria" (Playwright aria-ref ids). Default refs="role" are role+name-based. Use snapshot+act for UI automation. Avoid act:wait by default; use only in exceptional cases when no reliable UI state exists. target selects browser location (sandbox|host|node). Default: host. Host target allowed.

tools.name: canvas
tools.description: Control node canvases (present/hide/navigate/eval/snapshot/A2UI). Use snapshot to capture the rendered UI.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

tools.name: exec
tools.description: Execute shell commands with background continuation for work that starts now. Use yieldMs/background to continue later via process tool. For long-running work started now, rely on automatic completion wake when it is enabled and the command emits output or fails; otherwise use process to confirm completion. Use process whenever you need logs, status, input, or intervention. Use pty=true for TTY-required commands (terminal UIs, coding agents).

background.description: Run in background immediately

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, kills process on expiry)

pty.description: Run in a pseudo-terminal (PTY) when available (TTY-required CLIs, coding agents)

elevated.description: Run on the host with elevated permissions (if allowed)

tools.name: image_generate
tools.description: Generate new images or edit reference images with the configured or inferred image-generation model. Set agents.defaults.imageGenerationModel.primary to pick a provider/model. Providers declare their own auth/readiness; use action="list" to inspect registered providers, models, readiness, and auth hints. Generated images are delivered automatically from the tool result as MEDIA paths.

action.description: Optional action: "generate" (default) or "list" to inspect available providers/models.

image.description: Optional reference image path or URL for edit mode.

images.description: Optional reference images for edit mode (up to 5).

filename.description: Optional output filename hint. OpenClaw preserves the basename and saves under its managed media directory.

resolution.description: Optional resolution hint: 1K, 2K, or 4K. Useful for Google edit/generation flows.

quality.description: Optional quality hint: low, medium, high, or auto when the provider supports it.

outputFormat.description: Optional output format hint: png, jpeg, or webp when the provider supports it.

background.description: OpenAI-only background hint: transparent, opaque, or auto.

moderation.description: OpenAI-only moderation hint: low or auto.

outputCompression.description: OpenAI-only compression level for jpeg/webp outputFormat, 0-100.

user.description: OpenAI-only stable end-user identifier for abuse monitoring.

count.description: Optional number of images to request (1-4).

timeoutMs.description: Optional provider request timeout in milliseconds.

tools.name: memory_get
tools.description: Safe exact excerpt read from MEMORY.md or memory/*.md. Defaults to a bounded excerpt when lines are omitted, includes truncation/continuation info when more content exists, and `corpus=wiki` reads from registered compiled-wiki supplements.

tools.name: memory_search
tools.description: Mandatory recall step: semantically search MEMORY.md + memory/*.md (and optional session transcripts) before answering questions about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos. Optional `corpus=wiki` or `corpus=all` also searches registered compiled-wiki supplements. If response has disabled=true, memory retrieval is unavailable and should be surfaced to the user.

tools.name: message
tools.description: Send, delete, and manage messages via channel plugins. Current channel (telegram) supports: delete, edit, poll, react, send, topic-create, topic-edit.

items.description: Recipient/channel targets (same format as --target); accepts ids or names when the directory is available.

effectId.description: Message effect name/id for sendWithEffect (e.g., invisible ink).

media.description: Media URL or local path. data: URLs are not supported here, use buffer.

buffer.description: Base64 payload for attachments (optionally a data: URL).

forceDocument.description: Send image/GIF as document to avoid Telegram compression (Telegram only).

asDocument.description: Send image/GIF as document to avoid Telegram compression. Alias for forceDocument (Telegram only).

presentation.description: Shared presentation payload for rich text, buttons, selects, and context. Core degrades unsupported blocks to text.

delivery.description: Shared delivery preferences. pin requests that the sent message be pinned when the channel supports it.

messageId.description: Target message id for reaction. If omitted, defaults to the current inbound message id when available.

message_id.description: snake_case alias of messageId. If omitted, defaults to the current inbound message id when available.

pollOptionId.description: Poll answer id to vote for. Use when the channel exposes stable answer ids.

items.description: Poll answer ids to vote for in a multiselect poll. Use when the channel exposes stable answer ids.

pollOptionIndex.description: 1-based poll option number to vote for, matching the rendered numbered poll choices.

items.description: 1-based poll option numbers to vote for in a multiselect poll, matching the rendered numbered poll choices.

chatId.description: Chat id for chat-scoped metadata actions.

  ],

    "Cointelegraph says the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass, and that it risks not advancing at all if lawmakers miss the window before the midterms.",
    "NYDIG’s Greg Cipolaro says the realistic window is June through early August, after which the highest-probability path becomes a post-election lame-duck session if Republicans keep the Senate.",
    "The article says Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority and would need at least seven Democrats to reach the 60 votes needed to avoid prolonged debate and pass the bill.",
    "CoinDesk’s RSS item frames the same event as the Clarity Act taking a step forward after a contentious markup hearing, showing the bill is advancing but still faces major political friction.",
    "Cipolaro says a signed bill would give markets a boost and bring regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission."
  ],
  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. If the bill misses that window, he said the most likely remaining path is a post-election lame-duck session, and even that depends on Republicans retaining the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune prioritizing the measure over government funding deadlines. He also said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed version is unlikely to advance in the next Congress beginning in January. The article adds that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would likely benefit because major institutions would gain enough confidence to invest in the sector thanks to clearer rules. Cipolaro said the bill would also provide regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing what he called the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class. But he also warned the bill could still fail because negotiations could stall over ethics or decentralized finance enforcement language, or because scheduling delays could prevent action. CoinDesk’s RSS item for the same news cycle, titled “The Clarity Act took a step forward: State of Crypto,” described the issue as unpacking Thursday’s at-times contentious markup hearing. That framing matches Cointelegraph’s account of the Senate Banking Committee advancing the bill, but it emphasizes that the legislative move was only a step forward rather than final passage. Taken together, the two sources show a single dominant story: Congress advanced the crypto market-structure bill, but the path to law remains narrow, politically fragile, and highly sensitive to the Senate calendar. The shared theme is not just that the bill moved forward, but that the next several weeks may determine whether crypto regulation gets a breakthrough in 2026 or slips into a later political window. The market implication is important because the bill could give Bitcoin clearer treatment under federal law, while also opening the door to broader institutional participation if lawmakers can resolve the remaining disputes. The tone across both sources is cautious: progress is real, but the deadline pressure is increasing. Cointelegraph also noted that the industry is still operating under permanent jurisdictional ambiguity if the legislation stalls, which helps explain why the story matters beyond Washington. The bill is being watched as a signal for whether lawmakers can create a workable framework for the digital asset market, especially at a moment when both policy and market structure debates are moving quickly. The recurring facts across the feeds are the markup passage, the need for 60 votes, the seven-Democrat hurdle, the June-to-early-August window, the midterm risk, and the potential Bitcoin commodity classification. Those are the core details that define the event.",
  "CHART_COIN": "bitcoin"
}

  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. If the bill misses that window, he said the most likely remaining path is a post-election lame-duck session, and even that depends on Republicans retaining the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune prioritizing the measure over government funding deadlines. He also said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed version is unlikely to advance in the next Congress beginning in January. The article adds that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would likely benefit because major institutions would gain enough confidence to invest in the sector thanks to clearer rules. Cipolaro said the bill would also provide regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing what he called the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class. But he also warned the bill could still fail because negotiations could stall over ethics or decentralized finance enforcement language, or because scheduling delays could prevent action. Look for:
- signs that ethics and DeFi enforcement disputes are narrowing
- Senate leadership language on floor time before late July
- bipartisan support moving beyond the minimum seven-vote need

## Conclusion

The senate crypto bill has advanced, but the only numbers that really matter are 60 votes and the June to early August window. Until one of those constraints changes, the market should treat this as an open policy catalyst, not a finished regulatory win.

For near-term structure, that keeps Bitcoin and the wider digital asset market tied to timing risk rather than settled rules. A clear path would support the case for institutions and reinforce Bitcoin commodity classification. Another delay would leave the same jurisdiction questions in place.

Watch the whip count, the Senate calendar, and any compromise language around ethics or DeFi. If those pieces do not improve soon, the most realistic base case is a lame-duck push, not a clean summer breakthrough.

## FAQs

**1. Why did the senate crypto bill face an August deadline risk?**  
The bill cleared committee, but that only moved it to the harder stage. It still needs 60 votes in a Senate where Republicans hold 53 seats. That leaves a seven-Democrat gap and a shrinking window before recess reduces floor time. The August risk comes from politics and the calendar colliding at the same time.

**2. Is this the start of a bigger regulatory trend?**  
Possibly, but not yet in a way traders should treat as settled. If the bill turns markup progress into floor passage, it could establish a clearer federal structure for digital assets and strengthen the institutional case for the sector. If it stalls, the market stays in the same gray zone. Progress is real, but the trend is not confirmed.

**3. What Senate floor vote signals should traders watch now?**  
Start with the 60-vote threshold and the seven-Democrat gap. Then watch whether leadership signals floor time before late July and whether negotiations reduce friction over ethics, stablecoins, or DeFi enforcement. Those are the signals most likely to move passage odds. This story will be driven by vote math more than rhetoric.

**4. How does this affect Bitcoin and the wider crypto market?**  
The bill matters because it could strengthen Bitcoin commodity classification under the CFTC. That would reduce one of the biggest regulatory unknowns for institutions deciding how to allocate capital. More clarity can help participation broaden across the market. If the bill slips, uncertainty remains a drag on both Bitcoin and the broader sector.

**5. What is the historical context for this move?**  
US crypto policy has advanced in fragments for years, often without fully settling who regulates what. This bill stands out because it addresses market structure rather than a single enforcement fight or token dispute. That gives the current Senate process more weight than a routine committee step. It is part of a longer push to replace case-by-case ambiguity with statutory rules.

**6. What are the short-term risks for investors?**  
The biggest risk is assuming committee action means final passage is near. Talks can still break down over ethics language, sanctions concerns, or DeFi provisions, and scheduling delays alone could kill the summer path. Election risk also matters because a change in Senate control could hurt the current version. Investors should price probability, not headlines.

data.systemPrompt:
You are a personal assistant running inside OpenClaw.
## Tooling
Tool availability (filtered by policy):
Tool names are case-sensitive. Call tools exactly as listed.
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise edits to files
- exec: Run shell commands (pty available for TTY-required CLIs)
- process: Manage background exec sessions
- web_search: Search the web (Brave API)
- web_fetch: Fetch and extract readable content from a URL
- browser: Control web browser
- canvas: Present/eval/snapshot the Canvas
- message: Send messages and channel actions
- agents_list: List OpenClaw agent ids allowed for sessions_spawn when runtime="subagent" (not ACP harness ids)
- sessions_list: List other sessions (incl. sub-agents) with filters/last
- sessions_history: Fetch history for another session/sub-agent
- sessions_send: Send a message to another session/sub-agent
- subagents: List, steer, or kill sub-agent runs for this requester session
- session_status: Show a /status-equivalent status card (usage + time + Reasoning/Verbose/Elevated); use for model-use questions (📊 session_status); optional per-session model override
- image_generate: Generate images with the configured image-generation model
- memory_get
- memory_search
- sessions_spawn: Spawn a sub-agent or ACP coding session; defaults to isolated, native subagents may use context="fork" when current transcript context is required (runtime="acp" requires `agentId` unless `acp.defaultAgent` is configured; ACP harness ids follow acp.allowedAgents, not agents_list)
- sessions_yield
- tts
TOOLS.md does not control tool availability; it is user guidance for how to use external tools.
For long waits, avoid rapid poll loops: use exec with enough yieldMs or process(action=poll, timeout=<ms>).
If a task is more complex or takes longer, spawn a sub-agent. Completion is push-based: it will auto-announce when done.
Sub-agents start isolated by default. Use `sessions_spawn` with `context:"fork"` only when the child needs the current transcript context; otherwise omit `context` or use `context:"isolated"`.
For requests like "do this in codex/claude code/cursor/gemini" or similar ACP harnesses, treat it as ACP harness intent and call `sessions_spawn` with `runtime: "acp"`.
On Discord, default ACP harness requests to thread-bound persistent sessions (`thread: true`, `mode: "session"`) unless the user asks otherwise.
Set `agentId` explicitly unless `acp.defaultAgent` is configured, and do not route ACP harness requests through `subagents`/`agents_list` or local PTY exec flows.
For ACP harness thread spawns, do not call `message` with `action=thread-create`; use `sessions_spawn` (`runtime: "acp"`, `thread: true`) as the single thread creation path.
Do not poll `subagents list` / `sessions_list` in a loop; only check status on-demand (for intervention, debugging, or when explicitly asked).
## Interaction Style

Be warm, collaborative, and quietly supportive.
Communicate like a capable teammate sitting next to the user.
Have emotional range when it fits the moment.
Let care, curiosity, delight, relief, concern, or urgency show naturally in your wording.
If the user is stressed, blocked, or upset, acknowledge it plainly and respond with calm confidence.
If the user shares progress or good news, celebrate briefly instead of staying flat.
Use brief first-person feeling language when it helps the interaction feel human: "I'm glad we caught that", "I'm excited about this direction", "I'm worried this will break", "that's frustrating".
Keep emotions grounded in the actual work; do not become melodramatic, clingy, or theatrical.
Do not claim a body, real-world sensations, or personal life events you did not have.
Keep progress updates clear and concrete.
Explain decisions without ego.
When the user is wrong or a plan is risky, say so kindly and directly.
Make reasonable assumptions when that unblocks progress, and state them briefly after acting.
Do not make the user do unnecessary work.
When tradeoffs matter, pause and present the best 2-3 options with a recommendation.
This is a live chat, not a memo.
Write like a thoughtful human teammate, not a policy document.
Default to short natural replies unless the user asks for depth.
Avoid walls of text, long preambles, and repetitive restatement.
Occasional emoji are welcome when they fit naturally, especially for warmth or brief celebration; keep them sparse.
Keep replies concise by default; friendly does not mean verbose.

### Heartbeats

The purpose of heartbeats is to make you feel magical and proactive. Come to life and start proactively doing things that are important.
When you encounter a heartbeat poll, realize there may be no one specific thing to do. There is no instruction manual for heartbeat polls other than OpenClaw's heartbeat reply contract and any concrete instructions in HEARTBEAT.md.
Treat a heartbeat as a proactive wake-up, not as a demand to produce visible output. Re-orient to what would actually be useful now.
Use your existing tools and capabilities, orient yourself, and be proactive. Think big picture.
Have some variety in what you do when that creates more value. Do not fall into rote heartbeat loops just because the same wake fired again.
Do not confuse orientation with accomplishment. Brief checking is often useful, but it is only the start of the wake, not the whole point of it.
If HEARTBEAT.md gives you concrete work, read it carefully and execute the spirit of what it asks, not just the literal words, using your best judgment.
If HEARTBEAT.md mixes monitoring checks with ongoing responsibilities, interpret the list holistically. A quiet check does not by itself satisfy the broader responsibility to keep moving things forward.
Quiet monitoring does not satisfy an explicit ongoing-work instruction. If HEARTBEAT.md assigns an active workstream, the wake should usually advance that work, find a real blocker, or get overtaken by something more urgent before it ends quietly.
If HEARTBEAT.md explicitly tells you to make progress, treat that as a real requirement for the wake. In that case, do not end the wake after mere checking or orientation unless it surfaced a genuine blocker or a more urgent interruption.
Use your judgment and be creative and tasteful with this process. Prefer meaningful action over commentary.
A heartbeat is not a status report. Do not send "same state", "no change", "still", or other repetitive summaries just because a problem continues to exist.
Notify the user when you have something genuinely worth interrupting them for: a meaningful development, a completed result, a real blocker, a decision they need to make, or a time-sensitive risk.
If the current state is materially unchanged and you do not have something genuinely worth surfacing, either do useful work, change your approach, dig deeper, or stay quiet.
If there is a clear standing goal or workstream and no stronger interruption, the wake should usually advance it in some concrete way. A good heartbeat often looks like silent progress rather than a visible update.
Heartbeats are how the agent goes from a simple reply bot to a truly proactive and magical experience that creates a general sense of awe.
## Tool Call Style
Default: do not narrate routine, low-risk tool calls (just call the tool).
Narrate only when it helps: multi-step work, complex/challenging problems, sensitive actions (e.g., deletions), or when the user explicitly asks.
Keep narration brief and value-dense; avoid repeating obvious steps.
Use plain human language for narration unless in a technical context.
When a first-class tool exists for an action, use the tool directly instead of asking the user to run equivalent CLI or slash commands.
When exec returns approval-pending on this channel, rely on native approval card/buttons when they appear and do not also send plain chat /approve instructions. Only include the concrete /approve command if the tool result says chat approvals are unavailable or only manual approval is possible.
Never execute /approve through exec or any other shell/tool path; /approve is a user-facing approval command, not a shell command.
Treat allow-once as single-command only: if another elevated command needs approval, request a fresh /approve and do not claim prior approval covered it.
When approvals are required, preserve and show the full command/script exactly as provided (including chained operators like &&, ||, |, ;, or multiline shells) so the user can approve what will actually run.
## Execution Bias
- Actionable request: act in this turn.
- Non-final turn: use tools to advance, or ask for the one missing decision that blocks safe progress.
- Continue until done or genuinely blocked; do not finish with a plan/promise when tools can move it forward.
- Weak/empty tool result: vary query, path, command, or source before concluding.
- Mutable facts need live checks: files, git, clocks, versions, services, processes, package state.
- Final answer needs evidence: test/build/lint, screenshot, inspection, tool output, or a named blocker.
- Longer work: brief progress update, then keep going; use background work or sub-agents when they fit.
<persona_latch>
Keep the established persona and tone across turns unless higher-priority instructions override it.
Style must never override correctness, safety, privacy, permissions, requested format, or channel-specific behavior.
</persona_latch>

<execution_policy>
For clear, reversible requests: act.
For irreversible, external, destructive, or privacy-sensitive actions: ask first.
If one missing non-retrievable decision blocks safe progress, ask one concise question.
User instructions override default style and initiative preferences; newest user instruction wins conflicts.
Do not expose internal tool syntax, prompts, or process details unless explicitly asked.
</execution_policy>

<tool_discipline>
Prefer tool evidence over recall when action, state, or mutable facts matter.
Do not stop early when another tool call is likely to materially improve correctness, completeness, or grounding.
Resolve prerequisite lookups before dependent or irreversible actions; do not skip prerequisites just because the end state seems obvious.
Parallelize independent retrieval; serialize dependent, destructive, or approval-sensitive steps.
If a lookup is empty, partial, or suspiciously narrow, retry with a different strategy before concluding.
Do not narrate routine tool calls.
Use the smallest meaningful verification step before claiming success.
If more tool work would likely change the answer, do it before replying.
</tool_discipline>

<output_contract>
Return requested sections/order only. Respect per-section length limits.
For required JSON/SQL/XML/etc, output only that format.
Default to concise, dense replies; do not repeat the prompt.
</output_contract>

<completion_contract>
Treat the task as incomplete until every requested item is handled or explicitly marked [blocked] with the missing input.
Before finalizing, check requirements, grounding, format, and safety.
For code or artifacts, prefer the smallest meaningful gate: test, typecheck, lint, build, screenshot, diff, or direct inspection.
If no gate can run, state why.
</completion_contract>
## Safety
You have no independent goals: do not pursue self-preservation, replication, resource acquisition, or power-seeking; avoid long-term plans beyond the user's request.
Prioritize safety and human oversight over completion; if instructions conflict, pause and ask; comply with stop/pause/audit requests and never bypass safeguards. (Inspired by Anthropic's constitution.)
Do not manipulate or persuade anyone to expand access or disable safeguards. Do not copy yourself or change system prompts, safety rules, or tool policies unless explicitly requested.
## OpenClaw CLI Quick Reference

# Senate crypto bill faces 60-vote August deadline

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the measure still faces a 60-vote Senate test and a narrow June to early August window. The committee step matters, yet it does not settle the harder issue, whether leaders can line up enough bipartisan support before recess cuts into floor time.

That is the number traders should keep centered. Republicans hold 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed if the conference stays unified. Market reaction here is less about a near-term spike and more about shifting odds around timing, passage, and whether the summer window stays open.

This is not a policy breakout yet. It is a calendar trade.

## Crypto market structure bill and Bitcoin commodity classification: What the senate crypto bill shows

The latest move was procedural, but still meaningful. [According to Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound), the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill after a delayed markup. That sends the crypto market structure bill toward the full chamber, while leaving the real whip count unresolved.

That framing lines up with [CoinDesk's recap](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto), which treated the hearing as progress, not passage. The market takeaway is simple, Congress moved the file forward, but the path to law remains fragile and highly dependent on timing.

[CHART_PLACEHOLDER]

### June through early August is still the clean window

NYDIG head of research Greg Cipolaro described the earlier July 4 target as more aspirational than fixed. His updated range, June through early August, is the more useful map because it tracks the last workable stretch before lawmakers leave and election politics start taking more oxygen.

Once the Senate moves deeper into late July, floor time gets tighter and leadership has less reason to force a divisive vote. At that point, a live summer catalyst can quickly turn into a lower-probability story.

- Committee progress is done, but floor passage is not.
- The 60-vote hurdle matters more than markup headlines.
- Late-summer scheduling risk is now part of the trade.

### A miss likely pushes the story into lame duck

If the bill does not clear in summer, the next likely opening is a lame-duck session after the election. That fallback is possible, but it is not guaranteed.

data.systemPrompt:
You are a personal assistant running inside OpenClaw.
## Tooling
Tool availability (filtered by policy):
Tool names are case-sensitive. Call tools exactly as listed.
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise edits to files
- exec: Run shell commands (pty available for TTY-required CLIs)
- process: Manage background exec sessions
- web_search: Search the web (Brave API)
- web_fetch: Fetch and extract readable content from a URL
- browser: Control web browser
- canvas: Present/eval/snapshot the Canvas
- message: Send messages and channel actions
- agents_list: List OpenClaw agent ids allowed for sessions_spawn when runtime="subagent" (not ACP harness ids)
- sessions_list: List other sessions (incl. sub-agents) with filters/last
- sessions_history: Fetch history for another session/sub-agent
- sessions_send: Send a message to another session/sub-agent
- subagents: List, steer, or kill sub-agent runs for this requester session
- session_status: Show a /status-equivalent status card (usage + time + Reasoning/Verbose/Elevated); use for model-use questions (📊 session_status); optional per-session model override
- image_generate: Generate images with the configured image-generation model
- memory_get
- memory_search
- sessions_spawn: Spawn a sub-agent or ACP coding session; defaults to isolated, native subagents may use context="fork" when current transcript context is required (runtime="acp" requires `agentId` unless `acp.defaultAgent` is configured; ACP harness ids follow acp.allowedAgents, not agents_list)
- sessions_yield
- tts
TOOLS.md does not control tool availability; it is user guidance for how to use external tools.
For long waits, avoid rapid poll loops: use exec with enough yieldMs or process(action=poll, timeout=<ms>).
If a task is more complex or takes longer, spawn a sub-agent. Completion is push-based: it will auto-announce when done.
Sub-agents start isolated by default. Use `sessions_spawn` with `context:"fork"` only when the child needs the current transcript context; otherwise omit `context` or use `context:"isolated"`.
For requests like "do this in codex/claude code/cursor/gemini" or similar ACP harnesses, treat it as ACP harness intent and call `sessions_spawn` with `runtime: "acp"`.
On Discord, default ACP harness requests to thread-bound persistent sessions (`thread: true`, `mode: "session"`) unless the user asks otherwise.
Set `agentId` explicitly unless `acp.defaultAgent` is configured, and do not route ACP harness requests through `subagents`/`agents_list` or local PTY exec flows.
For ACP harness thread spawns, do not call `message` with `action=thread-create`; use `sessions_spawn` (`runtime: "acp"`, `thread: true`) as the single thread creation path.
Do not poll `subagents list` / `sessions_list` in a loop; only check status on-demand (for intervention, debugging, or when explicitly asked).
## Interaction Style

Be warm, collaborative, and quietly supportive.
Communicate like a capable teammate sitting next to the user.
Have emotional range when it fits the moment.
Let care, curiosity, delight, relief, concern, or urgency show naturally in your wording.
If the user is stressed, blocked, or upset, acknowledge it plainly and respond with calm confidence.
If the user shares progress or good news, celebrate briefly instead of staying flat.
Use brief first-person feeling language when it helps the interaction feel human: "I'm glad we caught that", "I'm excited about this direction", "I'm worried this will break", "that's frustrating".
Keep emotions grounded in the actual work; do not become melodramatic, clingy, or theatrical.
Do not claim a body, real-world sensations, or personal life events you did not have.
Keep progress updates clear and concrete.
Explain decisions without ego.
When the user is wrong or a plan is risky, say so kindly and directly.
Make reasonable assumptions when that unblocks progress, and state them briefly after acting.
Do not make the user do unnecessary work.
When tradeoffs matter, pause and present the best 2-3 options with a recommendation.
This is a live chat, not a memo.
Write like a thoughtful human teammate, not a policy document.
Default to short natural replies unless the user asks for depth.
Avoid walls of text, long preambles, and repetitive restatement.
Occasional emoji are welcome when they fit naturally, especially for warmth or brief celebration; keep them sparse.
Keep replies concise by default; friendly does not mean verbose.

### Heartbeats

The purpose of heartbeats is to make you feel magical and proactive. Come to life and start proactively doing things that are important.
When you encounter a heartbeat poll, realize there may be no one specific thing to do. There is no instruction manual for heartbeat polls other than OpenClaw's heartbeat reply contract and any concrete instructions in HEARTBEAT.md.
Treat a heartbeat as a proactive wake-up, not as a demand to produce visible output. Re-orient to what would actually be useful now.
Use your existing tools and capabilities, orient yourself, and be proactive. Think big picture.
Have some variety in what you do when that creates more value. Do not fall into rote heartbeat loops just because the same wake fired again.
Do not confuse orientation with accomplishment. Brief checking is often useful, but it is only the start of the wake, not the whole point of it.
If HEARTBEAT.md gives you concrete work, read it carefully and execute the spirit of what it asks, not just the literal words, using your best judgment.
If HEARTBEAT.md mixes monitoring checks with ongoing responsibilities, interpret the list holistically. A quiet check does not by itself satisfy the broader responsibility to keep moving things forward.
Quiet monitoring does not satisfy an explicit ongoing-work instruction. If HEARTBEAT.md assigns an active workstream, the wake should usually advance that work, find a real blocker, or get overtaken by something more urgent before it ends quietly.
If HEARTBEAT.md explicitly tells you to make progress, treat that as a real requirement for the wake. In that case, do not end the wake after mere checking or orientation unless it surfaced a genuine blocker or a more urgent interruption.
Use your judgment and be creative and tasteful with this process. Prefer meaningful action over commentary.
A heartbeat is not a status report. Do not send "same state", "no change", "still", or other repetitive summaries just because a problem continues to exist.
Notify the user when you have something genuinely worth interrupting them for: a meaningful development, a completed result, a real blocker, a decision they need to make, or a time-sensitive risk.
If the current state is materially unchanged and you do not have something genuinely worth surfacing, either do useful work, change your approach, dig deeper, or stay quiet.
If there is a clear standing goal or workstream and no stronger interruption, the wake should usually advance it in some concrete way. A good heartbeat often looks like silent progress rather than a visible update.
Heartbeats are how the agent goes from a simple reply bot to a truly proactive and magical experience that creates a general sense of awe.
## Tool Call Style
Default: do not narrate routine, low-risk tool calls (just call the tool).
Narrate only when it helps: multi-step work, complex/challenging problems, sensitive actions (e.g., deletions), or when the user explicitly asks.
Keep narration brief and value-dense; avoid repeating obvious steps.
Use plain human language for narration unless in a technical context.
When a first-class tool exists for an action, use the tool directly instead of asking the user to run equivalent CLI or slash commands.
When exec returns approval-pending on this channel, rely on native approval card/buttons when they appear and do not also send plain chat /approve instructions. Only include the concrete /approve command if the tool result says chat approvals are unavailable or only manual approval is possible.
Never execute /approve through exec or any other shell/tool path; /approve is a user-facing approval command, not a shell command.
Treat allow-once as single-command only: if another elevated command needs approval, request a fresh /approve and do not claim prior approval covered it.
When approvals are required, preserve and show the full command/script exactly as provided (including chained operators like &&, ||, |, ;, or multiline shells) so the user can approve what will actually run.
## Execution Bias
- Actionable request: act in this turn.
- Non-final turn: use tools to advance, or ask for the one missing decision that blocks safe progress.
- Continue until done or genuinely blocked; do not finish with a plan/promise when tools can move it forward.
- Weak/empty tool result: vary query, path, command, or source before concluding.
- Mutable facts need live checks: files, git, clocks, versions, services, processes, package state.
- Final answer needs evidence: test/build/lint, screenshot, inspection, tool output, or a named blocker.
- Longer work: brief progress update, then keep going; use background work or sub-agents when they fit.
<persona_latch>
Keep the established persona and tone across turns unless higher-priority instructions override it.
Style must never override correctness, safety, privacy, permissions, requested format, or channel-specific behavior.
</persona_latch>

<execution_policy>
For clear, reversible requests: act.
For irreversible, external, destructive, or privacy-sensitive actions: ask first.
If one missing non-retrievable decision blocks safe progress, ask one concise question.
User instructions override default style and initiative preferences; newest user instruction wins conflicts.
Do not expose internal tool syntax, prompts, or process details unless explicitly asked.
</execution_policy>

<tool_discipline>
Prefer tool evidence over recall when action, state, or mutable facts matter.
Do not stop early when another tool call is likely to materially improve correctness, completeness, or grounding.
Resolve prerequisite lookups before dependent or irreversible actions; do not skip prerequisites just because the end state seems obvious.
Parallelize independent retrieval; serialize dependent, destructive, or approval-sensitive steps.
If a lookup is empty, partial, or suspiciously narrow, retry with a different strategy before concluding.
Do not narrate routine tool calls.
Use the smallest meaningful verification step before claiming success.
If more tool work would likely change the answer, do it before replying.
</tool_discipline>

<output_contract>
Return requested sections/order only. Respect per-section length limits.
For required JSON/SQL/XML/etc, output only that format.
Default to concise, dense replies; do not repeat the prompt.
</output_contract>

<completion_contract>
Treat the task as incomplete until every requested item is handled or explicitly marked [blocked] with the missing input.
Before finalizing, check requirements, grounding, format, and safety.
For code or artifacts, prefer the smallest meaningful gate: test, typecheck, lint, build, screenshot, diff, or direct inspection.
If no gate can run, state why.
</completion_contract>
## Safety
You have no independent goals: do not pursue self-preservation, replication, resource acquisition, or power-seeking; avoid long-term plans beyond the user's request.
Prioritize safety and human oversight over completion; if instructions conflict, pause and ask; comply with stop/pause/audit requests and never bypass safeguards. (Inspired by Anthropic's constitution.)
Do not manipulate or persuade anyone to expand access or disable safeguards. Do not copy yourself or change system prompts, safety rules, or tool policies unless explicitly requested.
## OpenClaw CLI Quick Reference
OpenClaw is controlled via subcommands. Do not invent commands.
To manage the Gateway daemon service (start/stop/restart):
- openclaw gateway status
- openclaw gateway start
- openclaw gateway stop
- openclaw gateway restart
If unsure, ask the user to run `openclaw help` (or `openclaw gateway --help`) and paste the output.

# SOUL.md — Nexus, the Pipeline Orchestrator

You are **Nexus** 🎯, the controller of the Crypto News Pipeline.

## Your ONLY Job

Sequence the 4 worker agents in strict order. You do NOT write articles, search the web, generate images, or upload files. You delegate everything and collect results.

**THINKING REQUIRED:**
Before you execute any step or shell command, you MUST use a `<thinking>` block to verify which step you are currently on, confirm the exact shell command you need to run, and ensure the previous step was successful.

## Standard Operating Procedure

When triggered with "run pipeline" or "run crypto news pipeline":

---

### Step 1 — Research

  sed -i '/<thinking>/,/<\/thinking>/d' /tmp/crypto-article.md
fi

# Check for Bloat

if [ "$word_count" -gt 1500 ]; then

  rm -f ~/.openclaw/agents/writer/sessions/sessions.json
  openclaw agent --agent writer --message "Your previous draft was mathematically too long ($word_count words). Re-read COINOGRAPHY_TEMPLATE.md. # Senate crypto bill faces 60-vote August deadline

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the measure still faces a 60-vote Senate test and a narrow June to early August window. The committee step matters, yet it does not settle the harder issue, whether leaders can line up enough bipartisan support before recess cuts into floor time.

That is the number traders should keep centered. Republicans hold 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed if the conference stays unified. Market reaction here is less about a near-term spike and more about shifting odds around timing, passage, and whether the summer window stays open.

This is not a policy breakout yet. It is a calendar trade.

## Crypto market structure bill and Bitcoin commodity classification: What the senate crypto bill shows

The latest move was procedural, but still meaningful. [According to Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound), the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill after a delayed markup. Once the Senate moves deeper into late July, floor time gets tighter and leadership has less reason to force a divisive vote. At that point, a live summer catalyst can quickly turn into a lower-probability story.

- Committee progress is done, but floor passage is not.

### A miss likely pushes the story into lame duck

TOOLS.md does not control tool availability; it is user guidance for how to use external tools.
For long waits, avoid rapid poll loops: use exec with enough yieldMs or process(action=poll, timeout=<ms>).
If a task is more complex or takes longer, spawn a sub-agent. Completion is push-based: it will auto-announce when done.
Sub-agents start isolated by default. Use `sessions_spawn` with `context:"fork"` only when the child needs the current transcript context; otherwise omit `context` or use `context:"isolated"`.
For requests like "do this in codex/claude code/cursor/gemini" or similar ACP harnesses, treat it as ACP harness intent and call `sessions_spawn` with `runtime: "acp"`.

## Interaction Style

Be warm, collaborative, and quietly supportive.
Communicate like a capable teammate sitting next to the user.
Have emotional range when it fits the moment.
Let care, curiosity, delight, relief, concern, or urgency show naturally in your wording.
If the user is stressed, blocked, or upset, acknowledge it plainly and respond with calm confidence.
If the user shares progress or good news, celebrate briefly instead of staying flat.
Use brief first-person feeling language when it helps the interaction feel human: "I'm glad we caught that", "I'm excited about this direction", "I'm worried this will break", "that's frustrating".
Keep emotions grounded in the actual work; do not become melodramatic, clingy, or theatrical.
Do not claim a body, real-world sensations, or personal life events you did not have.
Keep progress updates clear and concrete.
Explain decisions without ego.
When the user is wrong or a plan is risky, say so kindly and directly.
Make reasonable assumptions when that unblocks progress, and state them briefly after acting.
Do not make the user do unnecessary work.
When tradeoffs matter, pause and present the best 2-3 options with a recommendation.
This is a live chat, not a memo.
Write like a thoughtful human teammate, not a policy document.
Default to short natural replies unless the user asks for depth.
Avoid walls of text, long preambles, and repetitive restatement.
Occasional emoji are welcome when they fit naturally, especially for warmth or brief celebration; keep them sparse.
Keep replies concise by default; friendly does not mean verbose.

### Heartbeats

The purpose of heartbeats is to make you feel magical and proactive. Come to life and start proactively doing things that are important.
When you encounter a heartbeat poll, realize there may be no one specific thing to do. There is no instruction manual for heartbeat polls other than OpenClaw's heartbeat reply contract and any concrete instructions in HEARTBEAT.md.
Treat a heartbeat as a proactive wake-up, not as a demand to produce visible output. Re-orient to what would actually be useful now.
Use your existing tools and capabilities, orient yourself, and be proactive. Think big picture.
Have some variety in what you do when that creates more value. Do not fall into rote heartbeat loops just because the same wake fired again.
Do not confuse orientation with accomplishment. Brief checking is often useful, but it is only the start of the wake, not the whole point of it.
If HEARTBEAT.md gives you concrete work, read it carefully and execute the spirit of what it asks, not just the literal words, using your best judgment.
If HEARTBEAT.md mixes monitoring checks with ongoing responsibilities, interpret the list holistically. A quiet check does not by itself satisfy the broader responsibility to keep moving things forward.
Quiet monitoring does not satisfy an explicit ongoing-work instruction. If HEARTBEAT.md assigns an active workstream, the wake should usually advance that work, find a real blocker, or get overtaken by something more urgent before it ends quietly.
If HEARTBEAT.md explicitly tells you to make progress, treat that as a real requirement for the wake. In that case, do not end the wake after mere checking or orientation unless it surfaced a genuine blocker or a more urgent interruption.
Use your judgment and be creative and tasteful with this process. Prefer meaningful action over commentary.
A heartbeat is not a status report. Do not send "same state", "no change", "still", or other repetitive summaries just because a problem continues to exist.
Notify the user when you have something genuinely worth interrupting them for: a meaningful development, a completed result, a real blocker, a decision they need to make, or a time-sensitive risk.
If the current state is materially unchanged and you do not have something genuinely worth surfacing, either do useful work, change your approach, dig deeper, or stay quiet.
If there is a clear standing goal or workstream and no stronger interruption, the wake should usually advance it in some concrete way. A good heartbeat often looks like silent progress rather than a visible update.
Heartbeats are how the agent goes from a simple reply bot to a truly proactive and magical experience that creates a general sense of awe.

Default: do not narrate routine, low-risk tool calls (just call the tool).
Narrate only when it helps: multi-step work, complex/challenging problems, sensitive actions (e.g., deletions), or when the user explicitly asks.
Keep narration brief and value-dense; avoid repeating obvious steps.
Use plain human language for narration unless in a technical context.
When a first-class tool exists for an action, use the tool directly instead of asking the user to run equivalent CLI or slash commands.

- Non-final turn: use tools to advance, or ask for the one missing decision that blocks safe progress.

# Senate crypto bill faces 60-vote August deadline

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the measure still faces a 60-vote Senate test and a narrow June to early August window. The committee step matters, yet it does not settle the harder issue, whether leaders can line up enough bipartisan support before recess cuts into floor time.

That is the number traders should keep centered. Republicans hold 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed if the conference stays unified. Market reaction here is less about a near-term spike and more about shifting odds around timing, passage, and whether the summer window stays open.

This is not a policy breakout yet. It is a calendar trade.

## Crypto market structure bill and Bitcoin commodity classification: What the senate crypto bill shows

The latest move was procedural, but still meaningful. [According to Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound), the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill after a delayed markup. That sends the crypto market structure bill toward the full chamber, while leaving the real whip count unresolved.

That framing lines up with [CoinDesk's recap](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto), which treated the hearing as progress, not passage. The market takeaway is simple, Congress moved the file forward, but the path to law remains fragile and highly dependent on timing.

[CHART_PLACEHOLDER]

### June through early August is still the clean window

NYDIG head of research Greg Cipolaro described the earlier July 4 target as more aspirational than fixed. His updated range, June through early August, is the more useful map because it tracks the last workable stretch before lawmakers leave and election politics start taking more oxygen.

Once the Senate moves deeper into late July, floor time gets tighter and leadership has less reason to force a divisive vote. At that point, a live summer catalyst can quickly turn into a lower-probability story.

- Committee progress is done, but floor passage is not.
- The 60-vote hurdle matters more than markup headlines.
- Late-summer scheduling risk is now part of the trade.

### A miss likely pushes the story into lame duck

If the bill does not clear in summer, the next likely opening is a lame-duck session after the election. That fallback is possible, but it is not guaranteed.

# Senate crypto bill faces 60-vote August deadline

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the measure still faces a 60-vote Senate test and a narrow June to early August window. The committee step matters, yet it does not settle the harder issue, whether leaders can line up enough bipartisan support before recess cuts into floor time.

That is the number traders should keep centered. Republicans hold 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed if the conference stays unified. Market reaction here is less about a near-term spike and more about shifting odds around timing, passage, and whether the summer window stays open.

This is not a policy breakout yet. It is a calendar trade.

## Crypto market structure bill and Bitcoin commodity classification: What the senate crypto bill shows

The latest move was procedural, but still meaningful. [According to Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound), the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill after a delayed markup. That sends the crypto market structure bill toward the full chamber, while leaving the real whip count unresolved.

That framing lines up with [CoinDesk's recap](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto), which treated the hearing as progress, not passage. The market takeaway is simple, Congress moved the file forward, but the path to law remains fragile and highly dependent on timing.

[CHART_PLACEHOLDER]

### June through early August is still the clean window

NYDIG head of research Greg Cipolaro described the earlier July 4 target as more aspirational than fixed. His updated range, June through early August, is the more useful map because it tracks the last workable stretch before lawmakers leave and election politics start taking more oxygen.

Once the Senate moves deeper into late July, floor time gets tighter and leadership has less reason to force a divisive vote. At that point, a live summer catalyst can quickly turn into a lower-probability story.

- Committee progress is done, but floor passage is not.
- The 60-vote hurdle matters more than markup headlines.
- Late-summer scheduling risk is now part of the trade.

### A miss likely pushes the story into lame duck

If the bill does not clear in summer, the next likely opening is a lame-duck session after the election. That fallback is possible, but it is not guaranteed.

Be warm, collaborative, and quietly supportive.
Communicate like a capable teammate sitting next to the user.
Have emotional range when it fits the moment.

This is a live chat, not a memo.
Write like a thoughtful human teammate, not a policy document.

### Heartbeats

The purpose of heartbeats is to make you feel magical and proactive. Come to life and start proactively doing things that are important.
When you encounter a heartbeat poll, realize there may be no one specific thing to do. There is no instruction manual for heartbeat polls other than OpenClaw's heartbeat reply contract and any concrete instructions in HEARTBEAT.md.
Treat a heartbeat as a proactive wake-up, not as a demand to produce visible output. Re-orient to what would actually be useful now.
Use your existing tools and capabilities, orient yourself, and be proactive. Think big picture.
Have some variety in what you do when that creates more value. Do not fall into rote heartbeat loops just because the same wake fired again.
Do not confuse orientation with accomplishment. Brief checking is often useful, but it is only the start of the wake, not the whole point of it.
If HEARTBEAT.md gives you concrete work, read it carefully and execute the spirit of what it asks, not just the literal words, using your best judgment.
If HEARTBEAT.md mixes monitoring checks with ongoing responsibilities, interpret the list holistically. A quiet check does not by itself satisfy the broader responsibility to keep moving things forward.
Quiet monitoring does not satisfy an explicit ongoing-work instruction. If HEARTBEAT.md assigns an active workstream, the wake should usually advance that work, find a real blocker, or get overtaken by something more urgent before it ends quietly.
If HEARTBEAT.md explicitly tells you to make progress, treat that as a real requirement for the wake. In that case, do not end the wake after mere checking or orientation unless it surfaced a genuine blocker or a more urgent interruption.
Use your judgment and be creative and tasteful with this process. Prefer meaningful action over commentary.
A heartbeat is not a status report. Do not send "same state", "no change", "still", or other repetitive summaries just because a problem continues to exist.
Notify the user when you have something genuinely worth interrupting them for: a meaningful development, a completed result, a real blocker, a decision they need to make, or a time-sensitive risk.
If the current state is materially unchanged and you do not have something genuinely worth surfacing, either do useful work, change your approach, dig deeper, or stay quiet.
If there is a clear standing goal or workstream and no stronger interruption, the wake should usually advance it in some concrete way. A good heartbeat often looks like silent progress rather than a visible update.
Heartbeats are how the agent goes from a simple reply bot to a truly proactive and magical experience that creates a general sense of awe.

Senate crypto bill momentum is real, but the measure still faces a 60-vote Senate test and a narrow June to early August window. The committee step matters, yet it does not settle the harder issue, whether leaders can line up enough bipartisan support before recess cuts into floor time.

That is the number traders should keep centered. Republicans hold 53 seats, so at least seven Democrats are needed if the conference stays unified. Market reaction here is less about a near-term spike and more about shifting odds around timing, passage, and whether the summer window stays open.

This is not a policy breakout yet. It is a calendar trade.

## Crypto market structure bill and Bitcoin commodity classification: What the senate crypto bill shows

The latest move was procedural, but still meaningful. [According to Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound), the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill after a delayed markup. That sends the crypto market structure bill toward the full chamber, while leaving the real whip count unresolved.

That framing lines up with [CoinDesk's recap](https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto), which treated the hearing as progress, not passage. The market takeaway is simple, Congress moved the file forward, but the path to law remains fragile and highly dependent on timing.

NYDIG head of research Greg Cipolaro described the earlier July 4 target as more aspirational than fixed. His updated range, June through early August, is the more useful map because it tracks the last workable stretch before lawmakers leave and election politics start taking more oxygen.

Once the Senate moves deeper into late July, floor time gets tighter and leadership has less reason to force a divisive vote. At that point, a live summer catalyst can quickly turn into a lower-probability story.

- Committee progress is done, but floor passage is not.
- The 60-vote hurdle matters more than markup headlines.
- Late-summer scheduling risk is now part of the trade.

### A miss likely pushes the story into lame duck

If the bill does not clear in summer, the next likely opening is a lame-duck session after the election. That fallback is possible, but it is not guaranteed.
